content: Tungiasis is a parasitic skin infestation caused by the Tunga penetrans flea, also known as the chigoe flea, jigger, nigua, or sand flea. This flea is predominantly found in tropical regions, including parts of Africa, the Caribbean, Central and South America, and India. The condition is endemic in countries such as Nigeria and Trinidad and Tobago, where, during the 1980s, the prevalence of tungiasis among children reached approximately 40%. Outside of these endemic areas, the disease is rarely encountered. The first documented case of tungiasis dates back to the 1500s, as reported by Gonzalez Fernandez De Oviedo y Valdes. This occurred when sailors from Christopher Columbus's ship, the Santa Maria, were shipwrecked on Haiti and subsequently became infected. Tungiasis also affected many soldiers of the Spanish conquistadors, who noted that an entire village in Colombia was abandoned due to the disease. The first clinical description of tungiasis was provided by the Portuguese physician Aleixo de Abreu. The symptoms of tungiasis include intense itching (pruritus), pain, inflammation, and swelling. Lesions and ulcerations are commonly observed, often with a characteristic black dot at the center of the lesion. If left untreated, secondary infections such as bacteremia, tetanus, and gangrene can develop, posing significant health risks. The most common sites of infection are the soles of the feet, the spaces between the toes, and the areas around the toenails. This is due to the limited jumping ability of the flea, which makes these areas more accessible. Preventing tungiasis is relatively straightforward and involves wearing shoes in endemic regions and treating infested soil with insecticides. Walking barefoot, particularly among children, remains the primary reason for the continued prevalence of tungiasis in impoverished, rural populations. Diagnosis of tungiasis is typically made through physical examination of the skin, with characteristic lesions being a key diagnostic feature. Treatment for tungiasis involves the physical removal of the flea using forceps or needles. Topical anti-parasitic medications can also be applied, and in some cases, surgical removal of the nodules may be necessary. Early detection allows for easier removal of the flea, although care must be taken to avoid rupturing the egg sac. The lesions often resemble pustules on the thick skin of the feet or hands. Other reported treatment methods include applying a thick wax, nail polish, or petroleum-based solutions to suffocate the flea. Cryotherapy, using liquid nitrogen to locally freeze the lesion, has also been successful. However, the use of substances such as formaldehyde, chloroform, and DDT is discouraged due to their potential side effects. Even without treatment, the embedded fleas will die within two weeks and are naturally shed as the skin undergoes its normal renewal process.
